paras.html: Calling-out power is not an emergency power: The deployment of the AFP and PNP to prevent or suppress lawless violence is a power that the Constitution directly vests in the President under Sec. 18, Art. VII. She does not need congressional authority to exercise it. It is distinct from emergency powers under Sec. 23(2), Art. VI, which require war or other national emergency and a law enacted by Congress.

paras.html: Deference on factual basis: The Court may inquire into the factual bases for the calling out of the armed forces, but it will generally defer to the President's judgment unless it is shown that the determination was attended by grave abuse of discretion. The petitioner bears the burden of proving that the President acted without factual basis (IBP v. Zamora).

paras.html: Amnesty distinguished from pardon: Pardon is granted by the Chief Executive alone, is a private act that must be pleaded and proved, is granted after conviction, and looks forward (it forgives the punishment). Amnesty is proclaimed by the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress, is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, is granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses (generally before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction), and looks backward: it abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself.
paras.text: Amnesty distinguished from pardon: Pardon is granted by the Chief Executive alone, is a private act that must be pleaded and proved, is granted after conviction, and looks forward (it forgives the punishment). Amnesty is proclaimed by the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress, is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, is granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses (generally before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction), and looks backward: it abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself.

paras.html: No admission required: To be entitled to the benefits of the Amnesty Proclamation, it is not necessary that the accused, as a condition precedent or sine qua non, admit having committed the offense and allege amnesty as a defense; it is sufficient that the evidence, either of the complainant or the accused, shows that the offense comes within the terms of the Proclamation.
paras.text: No admission required: To be entitled to the benefits of the Amnesty Proclamation, it is not necessary that the accused, as a condition precedent or sine qua non, admit having committed the offense and allege amnesty as a defense; it is sufficient that the evidence, either of the complainant or the accused, shows that the offense comes within the terms of the Proclamation.

paras.html: Non-waivable: Once established by the evidence, the right to the benefits of amnesty cannot be waived, because it is of public interest that one whom the law regards as innocent, and as a patriot or hero, is not punished as a criminal.

paras.html: Before the period for perfecting an appeal expired, Jimenez learned of Proclamation No. 8 (September 7, 1946), issued by President Manuel Roxas with the concurrence of Congress under Art. VII, Sec. 10, par. 6 of the Constitution [1935 Constitution].
paras.text: Before the period for perfecting an appeal expired, Jimenez learned of Proclamation No. 8 (September 7, 1946), issued by President Manuel Roxas with the concurrence of Congress under Art. VII, Sec. 10, par. 6 of the Constitution [1935 Constitution].

paras.html: Its operative part declares an amnesty in favor of:
paras.text: Its operative part declares an amnesty in favor of:

paras.html: "all persons who committed any act penalized under the Revised Penal Code in furtherance of the resistance to the enemy or against persons aiding in the war effort of the enemy, and committed during the period from December 8, 1941 to the date when each particular area of the Philippines was actually liberated from the enemy control and occupation. This amnesty shall not apply to crimes against chastity or to acts committed from purely personal motives."
paras.text: "all persons who committed any act penalized under the Revised Penal Code in furtherance of the resistance to the enemy or against persons aiding in the war effort of the enemy, and committed during the period from December 8, 1941 to the date when each particular area of the Philippines was actually liberated from the enemy control and occupation. This amnesty shall not apply to crimes against chastity or to acts committed from purely personal motives."

paras.html: Its whereas clauses state that the fact that such acts were committed in furtherance of the resistance is not a valid defense under Philippine law, and that the persons so accused "should not be regarded as criminals but rather as patriots and heroes".
paras.text: Its whereas clauses state that the fact that such acts were committed in furtherance of the resistance is not a valid defense under Philippine law, and that the persons so accused "should not be regarded as criminals but rather as patriots and heroes".

paras.html: It created Guerrilla Amnesty Commissions to examine the facts and circumstances surrounding each case and, if necessary, conduct summary hearings of witnesses for both the complainant and the accused. Upon finding that a case falls within the Proclamation, the Commission so declares, and the accused is forthwith released or discharged.
paras.text: It created Guerrilla Amnesty Commissions to examine the facts and circumstances surrounding each case and, if necessary, conduct summary hearings of witnesses for both the complainant and the accused. Upon finding that a case falls within the Proclamation, the Commission so declares, and the accused is forthwith released or discharged.

paras.html: Administrative Order No. 11 (October 2, 1946) created the Commissions: cases pending in the CFI of the province, and cases decided by the CFI but not yet elevated on appeal, go to the respective Amnesty Commission; cases pending appeal go to the Seventh Amnesty Commission.

paras.html: By Proclamation of the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress; a public act of which courts should take judicial notice.

paras.html: Granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses, generally before or after the institution of the criminal prosecution, and sometimes after conviction.

paras.html: Looks backward: abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself, so that the person released "stands before the law precisely as though he had committed no offense".

paras.html: Once established by the evidence (of the prosecution or of the defense), the right can not be waived, because it is of public interest that one whom the Proclamation, which has the force of a law, regards not only as innocent but as a patriot or hero cannot be punished as a criminal.

paras.html: A fortiori argument: courts cannot convict a person who, per the evidence, committed an act not punishable by law even if he confesses guilt; so also, they cannot convict one whom the law considers a patriot and hero.

paras.html: But although motive is a subjective state of mind, it need not be testified to by the defendant himself. It is generally established by witnesses' testimony on the acts or statements of the accused before or immediately after the offense, from which motive may be inferred.

paras.html: The accused's own statement at arraignment or hearing about his motive generally cannot be relied on, especially against contrary evidence, since it may be an afterthought or colored by his interest.

paras.html: Limits on the pardoning power are constitutional only: the power under Sec. 11(6), Art. VII (1935 Constitution) has two limitations, namely that it be exercised after conviction and that it does not extend to cases of impeachment. "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

VII (1935 Constitution) has two limitations, namely that it be exercised after conviction and that it does not extend to cases of impeachment. paras.html: Effect of an absolute pardon: "An absolute pardon not only blots out the crime committed, but removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction," including accessory and resultant disabilities. When granted after the term of imprisonment has expired, it removes all that is left of the consequences of conviction, such as a statutory disqualification from voting that rests on that conviction.

paras.html: The President and Congress act in tandem: Under Sec. 18, Art. VII, the President initiates the proclamation of martial law or the suspension of the writ, but only Congress can maintain it. Because congressional review is automatic, the Court must let Congress act first; the validity of the proclamation is "first a political question in the hands of Congress before it becomes a justiciable one in the hands of the Court." The Court steps in as the "final rampart" only when Congress defaults.

paras.html: Lifting before Congress acts moots the case: The withdrawal of Proc. 1959 after eight days, before the joint session could act and before it was meaningfully implemented, was a supervening event that obliterated any justiciable controversy. The exceptions to mootness did not apply, since the proclamation looked "more like saber-rattling than an actual deployment and arbitrary use of political power."

paras.html: The massacre and the state of emergency:
paras.text: The massacre and the state of emergency:

paras.html: On November 23, 2009, heavily armed men, believed led by the ruling Ampatuan family, gunned down 57 civilians on a highway in Ampatuan, Maguindanao, and buried them under shoveled dirt (the "Maguindanao massacre").
paras.text: On November 23, 2009, heavily armed men, believed led by the ruling Ampatuan family, gunned down 57 civilians on a highway in Ampatuan, Maguindanao, and buried them under shoveled dirt (the "Maguindanao massacre").

paras.html: Per the OSG's narration (quoted in J. Carpio's dissent): the convoy carried the wife and female relatives of Buluan Vice Mayor Esmael "Toto" Mangudadatu, lawyers, and media, on the way to file Mangudadatu's certificate of candidacy for Governor at the COMELEC office in Shariff Aguak. Mangudadatu had sent women and media believing they would deter an attack. About 100 armed men stopped the convoy at a PNP checkpoint and brought it to the hills of Brgy. Masalay; soldiers later found the bodies and three graves with a provincial-government backhoe nearby. Twenty-nine of the victims were media personnel; five victims were merely travelling on the same highway.

paras.html: On December 12, 2009, before Congress could act, PGMA issued Proclamation 1963, lifting martial law and restoring the writ in Maguindanao, eight days after Proc. 1959. Its whereas clauses stated that over 600 persons who allegedly rose publicly had surrendered or been arrested, that the areas held by armed groups had been cleared, that the courts and prosecutors' offices of Cotabato City had resumed work, and that the ARMM Vice-Governor had assumed as Acting Governor. Proc. 1946 (state of emergency) remained in force.

paras.html: In Resolutions of December 8 and 15, 2009, the Court consolidated the petitions and required comment. The December 15 Resolution posed six questions: mootness after Proc. 1963; whether "rebellion" in Sec. 18 means Art. 134 RPC rebellion; whether martial law/suspension authorizes warrantless arrests; whether the power is joint and sequential with Congress; which prevails if the Court and Congress conflict; and whether the Court's ruling is essential to related acts during martial law. The OSG also raised standing.

The OSG also raised standing.

paras.html: Standing

paras.html: Sec. 18 expressly gives "any citizen" standing, without distinction; per the Constitutional Commission deliberations, the citizen need not even be a taxpayer. The design is to arrest the grave effects of an illegal proclamation without delay.

paras.html: I. Mootness
paras.text: I. Mootness

paras.html: All four David v. Arroyo exceptions are present: (1) grave constitutional violation; (2) exceptional situation of paramount public interest (citing Fr. Bernas); (3) need for controlling principles, as this is the first case under the 1987 Constitution on martial law and suspension, a "rare opportunity"; (4) capable of repetition yet evading review.

paras.html: Voluntary cessation does not divest jurisdiction once a suit is filed (Province of North Cotabato v. GRP Peace Panel); the petitions were filed while Proc. 1959 was in effect.

paras.html: Dismissal "sets a very dangerous precedent": a President could impose martial law without basis and lift it before review to escape judicial rebuke.

paras.html: II. Meaning of "rebellion"
paras.text: II. Meaning of "rebellion"

paras.html: "Rebellion" in Sec. 18 has the same meaning as Art. 134 RPC: (1) Sec. 18's last paragraphs require persons to be "judicially charged" for rebellion, which presupposes a statute defining it, and the RPC is the only one; (2) it is the only meaning the people knew when they ratified the Constitution; (3) Proc. 1959's own whereas clause cites the RPC definition, as did Proc. 427 in SANLAKAS.
paras.text: "Rebellion" in Sec. 18 has the same meaning as Art. 134 RPC: (1) Sec. 18's last paragraphs require persons to be "judicially charged" for rebellion, which presupposes a statute defining it, and the RPC is the only one; (2) it is the only meaning the people knew when they ratified the Constitution; (3) Proc. 1959's own whereas clause cites the RPC definition, as did Proc. 427 in SANLAKAS.

paras.html: Standard of proof: not proof beyond reasonable doubt, clear and convincing evidence, preponderance, or substantial evidence, all of which would tie the President's hands; probable cause of the existence of rebellion suffices, consistent with "judicially charged."
paras.text: Standard of proof: not proof beyond reasonable doubt, clear and convincing evidence, preponderance, or substantial evidence, all of which would tie the President's hands; probable cause of the existence of rebellion suffices, consistent with "judicially charged."

paras.html: III. Warrantless arrests
paras.text: III. Warrantless arrests

paras.html: Martial law does not suspend the Constitution; the Bill of Rights stays operative. Warrantless arrests, searches, and seizures are valid only within Sec. 5, Rule 113 and the recognized exceptions (Pequet v. Tangonan). Suspension of the writ does not validate an illegal arrest; it only suspends the remedy of habeas corpus (Aberca v. Ver).

paras.html: IV. Not joint or sequential
paras.text: IV. Not joint or sequential

paras.html: The President's proclamation is complete by itself; Congress's power is to revoke, "not to confirm or ratify" — a veto, like the Court's review (amicus Mendoza). The Court may review even if Congress has not acted.

paras.html: A joint/sequential reading makes the 30-day deadline impossible, since Congress has no deadline and may simply let the proclamation lapse after 60 days. Lifting the proclamation only removes the urgency; it does not oust jurisdiction.

paras.html: V. Simultaneous review: three scenarios
paras.text: V. Simultaneous review: three scenarios

paras.html: (1) Court acts and Congress does not → no conflict; Court may annul. (2) Congress revokes first, on any ground → Court must respect it. (3) Court upholds first → Congress may still revoke, as its power is broader. This case falls under the first scenario.

paras.html: The 1987 Constitution requires an actual invasion or rebellion and public safety; it deliberately deleted "imminent danger" found in the 1935 and 1973 Constitutions.

paras.html: The President's alter egos negated an actual rebellion: ES Ermita conceded there may have been "no actual rebellion"; DOJ Sec. Devanadera spoke of a rebellion "in the offing" and "looming"; the AFP Chief of Staff spoke of an "imminent threat"; Def. Sec. Gonzales and DILG Sec. Puno doubted the need for martial law. A looming rebellion is the deleted "imminent danger."

paras.html: The Sec. 13, Art. VII ban covers acting designations: The prohibition against Members of the Cabinet, their deputies, and assistants holding any other office applies to all appointments or designations, whether permanent or temporary. "To hold an office" means to possess or occupy it, which implies the actual discharge of its functions and duties; Sec. 13 makes no reference to the nature of the appointment.
paras.text: The Sec. 13, Art. VII ban covers acting designations: The prohibition against Members of the Cabinet, their deputies, and assistants holding any other office applies to all appointments or designations, whether permanent or temporary. "To hold an office" means to possess or occupy it, which implies the actual discharge of its functions and duties; Sec. 13 makes no reference to the nature of the appointment.

paras.html: Exceptions are strictly confined: Officials under Sec. 13 may hold another office only where the Constitution itself so provides (e.g., the VP as a Cabinet member; the SOJ as ex officio JBC member) or in an ex officio capacity (by law, required by the primary functions of the principal office, and without additional compensation). They cannot invoke the broader exceptions of Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B ("unless otherwise allowed by law or the primary functions of his position"). The positions of Secretary of Justice and Solicitor General are not ex officio to each other.

paras.html: CLU Resolution (Aug. 1, 1991), as adverted to in Elma: "the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants" refers only to heads of executive departments, their undersecretaries, and assistant secretaries, not to officials merely given the rank of Secretary, Undersecretary, or Assistant Secretary. Hence Elma (Presidential Assistant with the rank of Undersecretary) was not covered by Sec. 13.

paras.html: Because of Sec. 13, Agra did not validly hold the position of Acting SOJ concurrently with Acting SolGen, so he was not a de jure officer for his entire tenure as Acting SOJ. A de jure officer is one deemed in all respects legally appointed and qualified and whose term has not expired (Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: CLU: officials in the questioned positions may be considered de facto officers and are entitled to emoluments for actual services rendered. Where there is no de jure officer, a de facto officer who in good faith possessed the office and discharged its duties may recover its salary, since "it seems unjust that the public should benefit by the services of an officer de facto and then be freed from all liability to pay."

paras.html: A de facto officer derives his appointment from one having colorable authority to appoint, and the appointment is valid on its face (Dimaandal v. COA). He may also be one in possession of an office and discharging its duties under color of authority, i.e., authority from an appointment however irregular or informal, so that he is not a mere volunteer (CSC v. Joson, Jr.).

paras.html: Members of the Constitutional Commissions fall under the general rule: Not being Cabinet officials, they are covered by Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B rather than Sec. 13, Art. VII, so they may hold another office or employment if allowed by law or by the primary functions of their position. An ex officio post is valid only if it is derived from the primary functions of the principal office and carries no additional compensation. Hence, Sec. 14, Ch. 3, Title I-A, Book V, EO 292 (CSC Chairman sits on boards of entities affecting the career and welfare of government employees) is constitutional.

paras.html: Ex officio designation beyond primary functions is void: Designating the CSC Chairman to the boards of the GSIS, PhilHealth, ECC, and HDMF is unconstitutional because those boards also exercise non-personnel corporate powers not derived from his position, and the designation entitles him to per diem, a form of additional compensation, in violation of Sec. 2, Art. IX-A.

paras.html: Jun. 6, 2011: RA 10149 (GOCC Governance Act of 2011) took effect. Sec. 13 maintains the number of directors/trustees under the charters; Sec. 14 allows ex officio members to designate alternates; Sec. 15 requires appointive directors to be appointed by the President from a GCG shortlist; Sec. 17 sets one-year terms and gives incumbent appointive board members a term only until Jun. 30, 2011. The Court noted that Duque's designation "could have terminated or been rendered invalid" by RA 10149, rendering the petition moot.

paras.html: Sec. 1, Art. IX-A expressly describes the Commissions as "independent." Although their functions are essentially executive, they are not under the control of the President. Each conducts its own proceedings under its own rules and discretion, and its decisions are subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A; Brillantes, Jr. v. Yorac).

Each conducts its own proceedings under its own rules and discretion, and its decisions are subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A; Brillantes, Jr. v. Yorac).

paras.html: To safeguard independence, Sec. 2, Art. IX-A imposes disqualifications on the Chairmen and members: (a) holding any other office or employment during their tenure; (b) practicing any profession; (c) actively managing or controlling a business that may be affected by their functions; and (d) being financially interested in any government contract, franchise, or privilege. This case involves (a).

paras.html: The Court also listed, citing Nachura, the other features that ensure independence: constitutional creation (not abolishable by statute); express independence; powers not reducible by statute; removal only by impeachment; seven-year terms; no reappointment or acting appointments; salaries not decreased; fiscal autonomy; own procedural rules; disqualifications; and power to appoint their own personnel.

paras.html: Ex officio (CLU): "from office; by virtue of office"; authority annexed to the official position; membership "by virtue of his title to a certain office, and without further warrant or appointment". Because the ex officio position is part of the principal office, the official has no right to additional compensation; his services are already paid by the compensation of the principal office.

"The Executive branch is unitary"; an executive office not under the President's control is a "lost command" without legal or constitutional basis.

paras.html: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.
paras.text: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.

paras.html: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.
paras.text: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.

paras.html: Aggregate seven-year limit; Matibag abandoned in part: No one may serve in the Commission, as Chairman, Commissioner, or both, for an aggregate of more than seven years. The fourth situation in Matibag v. Benipayo (barring the reappointment of one who served less than seven years to an unexpired term) is obiter and is abandoned.

paras.html: A case is moot when its purpose has become stale or it ceases to present a justiciable controversy owing to supervening events, so that a resolution would be of no practical value. As a general rule, the Court does not decide moot cases.

paras.html: Republic v. Imperial: two conditions are indispensable to the rotational plan: (a) the first terms start on a common date; and (b) a vacancy from death, resignation, or disability is filled only for the unexpired balance. Its purpose: to prevent a four-year administration from appointing more than one permanent commissioner, or, per CONCOM Commissioner Monsod, "to prevent one person (the President of the Philippines) from dominating the commissions"; it also ensures continuity and independence.

paras.html: Vacancy by expiration vs. other causes. An appointment to a vacancy from expiration of a term is for seven years. There is an unexpired portion only when, because of death, disability, resignation, or impeachment, a sitting member cannot complete the term. Where the vacancy is from expiration, "there is technically no unexpired portion to speak of."

paras.html: Meaning of "reappointment." "Reappointment" means a second appointment to one and the same office (Sibal, citing Visarra). J. Dizon, dissenting in Visarra v. Miraflor: the ban refers to a second appointment to the same office; an occupant needs no second appointment unless he ceased to be the legal occupant. → A promotion, albeit entailing a second appointment, involves a different office and is not, strictly, a reappointment. J. Bautista, concurring in Visarra, likewise viewed a promotional appointment as not prohibited under the 1935 Constitution.

paras.html: No textual restriction? The command is that members are appointed "for a term of seven years" and appointment to a vacancy "shall be only for the unexpired portion." The President has two and only two options: a full seven years for a vacancy by expiration, or the unexpired term for a vacancy by death, disability, resignation, or impeachment. Otherwise the President could "trifle with terms of office fixed by the Constitution."

paras.html: Garcia precedent (1959). The promotion of COMELEC Commissioner Garcia to succeed Chairman Carag upon expiration of the latter's term, under the 1935 Constitution, is not a precedent under the 1987 Constitution. That it went uncontested does not matter: "the promotion in question was either legal or it was not. If it were not, no amount of repetitive practices would clear it of invalidating taint."

paras.html: Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D, 1987 Constitution: "The Chairman and Commissioners shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years without reappointment. Of those first appointed, the Chairman shall hold office for seven years, one Commissioner for five years, and the other Commissioner for three years, without reappointment. Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor. In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity." The identical rule governs the CSC and COMELEC.

paras.html: Rotational plan; common starting date: The rotational plan for the Constitutional Commissions requires that the terms of the first appointees start on a common date, irrespective of the variations in the dates of their appointments and qualification, and that any vacancy be filled only for the unexpired balance of the term (Republic v. Imperial). Under the 1987 Constitution, that common date is February 2, 1987, the date of ratification. In case of a belated appointment or qualification, the interval between the start of the term and actual qualification is counted against the appointee.

Imperial). Under the 1987 Constitution, that common date is February 2, 1987, the date of ratification. In case of a belated appointment or qualification, the interval between the start of the term and actual qualification is counted against the appointee.

paras.html: Term vs. tenure: The term is "the time during [which] the officer may claim to hold office as of right," and it fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another; the term is not affected by hold-over. Tenure is the period the incumbent actually holds office and may be shorter than the term. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII (transitory provision) governs the tenure of the incumbent commissioners, not the term under Art. IX.

paras.html: De facto officer: An appointee is bound by the term stated in the appointment she accepted; but one who stays beyond that term and serves as a de facto officer in good faith is entitled to her salary and emoluments for actual service rendered.

paras.html: Quoting Topacio Nueno v. Angeles (also citing Alba v. Evangelista, Paredes v. Abad, Aparri v. CA): "The term means the time during the officer may claim to hold office as of right, and fixes the interval after which the several incumbents shall succeed one another. The tenure represents the term during which the incumbent actually holds the office. The term of office is not affected by the hold-over. The tenure may be shorter than the term for reasons within or beyond the power of the incumbent."

paras.html: "Unless" imports an exception to the general rule (Tajanlangit v. Cazeñas). The incumbents continue for one year under their existing appointments at the discretion of the appointing power, who may cut their tenure short by (1) removal for cause, (2) incapacity, or (3) appointment to a new term, all of which may happen before the one-year period ends.

paras.html: "WHEREFORE, we adjudge that the term of office of Ms. Thelma P. Gaminde as Commissioner, Civil Service Commission, under an appointment extended to her by President Fidel V. Ramos on June 11, 1993, expired on February 02, 1999. However, she served as de facto officer in good faith until February 02, 2000, and thus entitled to receive her salary and other emoluments for actual service rendered. Consequently, the Commission on Audit erred in disallowing in audit such salary and other emoluments, including that of her co-terminous staff.

paras.html: Calling-out power is reviewable only for grave abuse: The President has full discretion to call out the armed forces "whenever it becomes necessary" to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion or rebellion. Unlike martial law and the suspension of the writ, there is no provision for congressional revocation or SC review of the sufficiency of its factual basis. The Court may only ask whether the power was exercised within constitutional limits or with grave abuse of discretion, and the petitioner must show that the President's decision is "totally bereft of factual basis."

paras.html: In view of the alarming increase in violent crimes in Metro Manila (robberies, kidnappings, carnappings), President Joseph Ejercito Estrada, in a verbal directive, ordered the PNP and the Philippine Marines to conduct joint visibility patrols for crime prevention and suppression.
paras.text: In view of the alarming increase in violent crimes in Metro Manila (robberies, kidnappings, carnappings), President Joseph Ejercito Estrada, in a verbal directive, ordered the PNP and the Philippine Marines to conduct joint visibility patrols for crime prevention and suppression.

paras.html: The Secretary of National Defense, the AFP Chief of Staff, the PNP Chief, and the SILG were tasked to execute and implement the order.
paras.text: The Secretary of National Defense, the AFP Chief of Staff, the PNP Chief, and the SILG were tasked to execute and implement the order.

paras.html: In compliance, the PNP Chief, through Police Chief Superintendent Edgar B. Aglipay, formulated Letter of Instruction (LOI) 02/2000, detailing how the patrols, called Task Force Tulungan, would be conducted. The Task Force was placed under the leadership of the Police Chief of Metro Manila.

paras.html: Requisites: (1) an actual and appropriate case; (2) a personal and substantial interest of the party raising the constitutional question; (3) judicial review pleaded at the earliest opportunity; (4) the constitutional question is the lis mota (PHILCONSA v. Enriquez).

Cuenco); cf. the Baker v. Carr factors, led by a "textually demonstrable constitutional commitment of the issue to a coordinate political department."

paras.html: Structure of Sec. 18: Congress may revoke, and the SC may review the sufficiency of the factual basis of, martial law and the suspension of the writ only. There is no equivalent provision for the calling-out power → it is in a different category; otherwise the framers would have lumped the three powers together. Expressio unius est exclusio alterius (Sarmiento v. Mison).

Bernas described a "graduated power": calling out, then suspension, then martial law; the first two greater powers are subject to review, but when the President exercises the "lesser power of calling on the Armed Forces … his judgment cannot be reviewed by anybody." Comm. Regalado: calling out does not require legislative concurrence "nor is it subject to judicial review."

paras.html: Why the difference: calling out is the lesser and more benign power; suspension and martial law curtail basic civil rights and so need congressional safeguards and judicial review.

paras.html: Every successor gets a full seven-year term: Harmonizing Sec. 11, Art. XI with Sec. 8(3) of RA 6770, “in any vacancy for the positions of Ombudsman and the deputies, whether as a result of the expiration of the term or death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the predecessor, the successor shall always be appointed for a full term of seven years.” The term is reckoned from the date of appointment, not from 2 February 1987.
paras.text: Every successor gets a full seven-year term: Harmonizing Sec. 11, Art. XI with Sec. 8(3) of RA 6770, “in any vacancy for the positions of Ombudsman and the deputies, whether as a result of the expiration of the term or death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the predecessor, the successor shall always be appointed for a full term of seven years.” The term is reckoned from the date of appointment, not from 2 February 1987.

paras.html: Rank and salary only: Sec. 10, Art. XI equates the Ombudsman and the Deputies with the Chairman and Members of the Constitutional Commissions only as to rank and salary, not term of office. The Office of the Ombudsman is not a constitutional commission (it is not a collegial body), so the 7-5-3 rotational plan and the Gaminde ruling do not apply to it.

paras.html: Ordinary meaning: “salary” is a recompense for services; “rank” is a designation fixing an officer's relative position in privilege, precedence, command, or pay. Neither includes “term of office”, i.e., the time during which the officer may claim to hold office as of right, which fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another (Fetalino v. COMELEC, citing Nueno v. Angeles).

paras.html: Republic v. Imperial (1955): the plan aims to keep one seat vacant every three years so that no President can appoint more than one commissioner. It has two indispensable conditions: (1) the first terms start on a common date; and (2) vacancies are filled only for the unexpired balance.

paras.html: The plan was carried into the CSC, COMELEC, and COA under Art. XII of the 1973 Constitution (7-5-3) and Sec. 1(2), Arts. IX-B, IX-C, and IX-D of the 1987 Constitution. The first terms start on a common date, regardless of appointment dates, so that a regular two-year interval recurs.

paras.html: Gaminde v. COA: Gaminde was appointed ad interim CSC Commissioner on 11 June 1993 (assumed 22 June 1993); her appointment paper said her term would expire on 2 February 1999. The COA disallowed her salaries after that date. The SC held her term expired on 2 February 1999: the first appointees' staggered 7-5-3 terms began on 2 February 1987, and any delay in appointment or qualification is counted against the appointee. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII concerns tenure, not term.

paras.html: Habeas corpus has very limited availability as a post-conviction remedy: review of a judgment of conviction via habeas corpus is allowed only when, as a consequence of a judicial proceeding, (a) there has been a deprivation of a constitutional right resulting in the restraint of a person; (b) the court had no jurisdiction to impose the sentence; or (c) an excessive penalty has been imposed, as such sentence is void as to the excess (Feria v. CA).

CA).

paras.html: Habeas corpus is not a writ of error: it permits a collateral challenge to the jurisdiction of the court, not a review of mere errors of fact or law committed within jurisdiction; "a habeas corpus petition reaches the body, but not the record of the case" (Velasco v. CA). A denial of a constitutional right ousts the court of jurisdiction, so the void judgment may be collaterally attacked through habeas corpus (Chavez v. CA; Gumabon).

paras.html: In an information dated January 9, 1995, filed with the RTC of Pasig City, Aileen Mendoza charged petitioner Reynaldo de Villa, her uncle by affinity (she was his niece by affinity), with rape. He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment on January 26, 1995.
paras.text: In an information dated January 9, 1995, filed with the RTC of Pasig City, Aileen Mendoza charged petitioner Reynaldo de Villa, her uncle by affinity (she was his niece by affinity), with rape. He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment on January 26, 1995.

paras.html: Prosecution's version: In the third week of April 1994, at about 10:00 a.m., Aileen, then 12 years and ten months old, woke up in her family's rented room in Sagad, Pasig, to find petitioner on top of her. He covered her mouth with a pillow and threatened to kill her, so she could only cry. He inserted his penis into her vagina, made thrusting motions, and ejaculated.

paras.html: Her mother, Leonila Mendoza, noticed Aileen's pregnancy in November 1994. Confronted, Aileen revealed that petitioner had raped her, and her parents filed a complaint at the Pasig Police Station.

paras.html: Dr. Rosaline Cosidon confirmed that Aileen was eight months pregnant and found healed hymenal lacerations at the 5:00 and 8:00 positions. On December 19, 1994, Aileen gave birth to a baby girl, Leahlyn Mendoza.

paras.html: Defense: Petitioner was 67 years old at the time; old age and sickness had rendered him incapable of an erection; Aileen's family held a grudge against him; and alibi: he was in his hometown of San Luis, Batangas.

paras.html: SC on automatic review: the child's date of birth was medically consistent with the time of the rape; since it was never alleged that Aileen gave birth to a full-term baby, the Court credited the prosecution's claim of a premature, eight-month baby by normal delivery. By Decision dated February 1, 2001, the Court affirmed the conviction for rape with modifications: reclusión perpetua; ₱50,000.00 civil indemnity; ₱50,000.00 moral damages; costs; and support for the child Leahlyn Corales Mendoza.

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to dismiss. The DNA evidence here is not material and relevant to the crime of rape: even assuming petitioner is not the father of the child conceived within the period of the rape, that does not prove he could not have committed the crime, so habeas corpus and new trial are unavailing. But the case should not close the door to a convict who, after final judgment, obtains DNA results that exonerate him.

paras.html: Before post-conviction DNA statutes, US courts required the convict to apply for testing; once the result confirmed innocence, they held a motion *in limine* hearing on admissibility or ordered a new trial; the prosecution usually declined to re-try, and the convict was released.
paras.text: Before post-conviction DNA statutes, US courts required the convict to apply for testing; once the result confirmed innocence, they held a motion *in limine* hearing on admissibility or ordered a new trial; the prosecution usually declined to re-try, and the convict was released.

paras.html: Relief came through habeas corpus and new trial, both with built-in limits (a constitutional violation at trial; newly discovered and not time-barred evidence), so courts granted it restrictively, case by case.

paras.html: Summerville v. Warden (Conn. 1994): evidence so strong that innocence is highly likely is itself a basis for habeas review → new trial on a claim of actual innocence. People v. Callace (N.Y. 1991): DNA testing is newly discovered evidence because that type of analysis was not available at trial. State v. Thomas (N.J. 1991): fundamental fairness allowed testing even though the request was stale.

paras.html: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).
paras.text: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).

paras.html: Parameters: There must be (1) actual rebellion or invasion (rebellion as defined in Art. 134, RPC) and (2) a public safety requirement, concurring. The President needs only probable cause to believe rebellion exists. Review covers only facts known to the President at the time of the proclamation (in the Proclamation and the Report), taken in totality, for sufficiency, not accuracy; the Court does not calibrate the President's choice among his graduated powers.

paras.html: Territorial scope: The Constitution leaves to the President whether to place "the Philippines or any part thereof" under martial law. Because rebellion "cannot be confined a priori within predetermined bounds", martial law over the whole of Mindanao was upheld. Terrorism neither negates nor absorbs rebellion.

paras.html: Sep. 4, 2016: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 55, declaring a state of national emergency on account of lawless violence in Mindanao.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: A government operation to capture Isnilon Hapilon (ASG leader) and Maute Group leaders Abdullah and Omarkhayam Maute met armed resistance that escalated into open hostility in Marawi City. Per the President's Report: at 2:00 PM, the Maute Group and ASG attacked government and private facilities; at 4:00 PM, about 50 armed men assaulted the Marawi City Jail and freed at least 68 inmates; power was cut citywide; the Marawi Police Station was ambushed and burned; three bridges fell under their control; checkpoints were set up at the Iligan–Marawi junction; Dansalan College, the Cathedral of Maria Auxiliadora, and other buildings were burned and hostages taken; the Maute Group reportedly took over Amai Pakpak Hospital and hoisted the DAESH/ISIS flag; about 75% of Marawi was reportedly infiltrated; 11 soldiers and police were killed and 35 wounded.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: Proclamation No. 216 declared martial law and suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the "Mindanao group of islands" for not more than 60 days. It was "DONE in the Russian Federation." Its key Whereas clauses:
paras.text: May 23, 2017: Proclamation No. 216 declared martial law and suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the "Mindanao group of islands" for not more than 60 days. It was "DONE in the Russian Federation." Its key Whereas clauses:

paras.html: "WHEREAS, today 23 May 2017, the same Maute terrorist group has taken over a hospital in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, established several checkpoints within the City, burned down certain government and private facilities and inflicted casualties on the part of Government forces, and started flying the flag of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) in several areas, thereby openly attempting to remove from the allegiance to the Philippine Government this part of Mindanao and deprive the Chief Executive of his powers and prerogatives . . . constituting the crime of rebellion; and WHEREAS, this recent attack shows the capability of the Maute group and other rebel groups to sow terror, and cause death and damage to property not only in Lanao del Sur but also in other parts of Mindanao."

paras.html: May 25, 2017: The President submitted a written Report to Congress: Mindanao as a "hotbed of violent extremism" (Zamboanga siege, Davao bombing, Mamasapano, bombings in Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Basilan); the ASG and the ISIS-backed Maute Group (263 members) aiming to establish a DAESH wilayat in Mindanao; Marawi's strategic location; and that public safety required martial law "in the whole of Mindanao until such time that the rebellion is completely quelled."

paras.html: After briefings, the Senate adopted P.S. Resolution No. 388 (Proclamation "satisfactory, constitutional and in accordance with the law"; "no compelling reason to revoke"), and the House adopted House Resolution No. 1050 (full support; "no reason to revoke").

paras.html: Jun. 5, 2017 – G.R. No. 231658 (Lagman): Five Representatives filed a petition under the third paragraph of Sec. 18, Art. VII, arguing: (1) no rebellion, only terrorism; the Maute Group is a "private militia"; the ISIS flag is propaganda; the conflict was precipitated by the government's bid to capture Hapilon, so at most there is an "imminent danger" of rebellion, no longer a ground; (2) the Report contained "false, inaccurate, contrived and hyperbolic accounts" (Amai Pakpak Hospital, Landbank, schools, police chief beheading, city hall); (3) it included old, resolved events (Butig, the 2016 jailbreak, Zamboanga, Davao, Mamasapano); (4) the President acted alone without consulting the military; and (5) the military had pre-empted the plan; no MILF hostility; foreign fighters "undetermined."

paras.html: Lansang (1935 Constitution) applied a "prudentially narrow test of arbitrariness." The 1987 Constitution, by providing for review of sufficiency of the factual bases, "has in fact done away with the test of arbitrariness". Under contemporaneous construction, "sufficiency of factual basis" is the only test: the Court need not be satisfied that the decision is correct, only that it had sufficient factual bases.

paras.html: Public safety is abstract and has no physical metes and bounds. Under the absorption doctrine (Hernandez, Dasig), crimes committed elsewhere in furtherance of rebellion (e.g., a murder in Makati) are part of the rebellion → territorial scope cannot be fixed in proportion to the "range" of rebellion. Limiting martial law to the place of actual fighting would let rebels escape and keep their supply lines.

paras.html: Actual rebellion only in Marawi: the 400–500 armed Maute-Hapilon fighters' uprising in Marawi is indisputable rebellion, but the Proclamation itself speaks of removing "this part of Mindanao", and the Report calls Marawi a "precedent" to spreading control: an admission that the rebellion had yet to spread. No evidence of rebellion in Camiguin, Dinagat, Bukidnon, and elsewhere.

paras.html: BERSAMIN, J.: The 1987 Constitution reverts to the traditional, theater-of-war concept of martial law (Ex parte Milligan; Duncan v. Kahanamoku). Agrees the proceeding is sui generis and the Court acts as a trier of facts; requiring grave abuse could void a proclamation with nine false bases out of ten despite one true basis. The burden is on petitioners (presumptions of constitutionality and good faith), but suggests that specific denials could shift the burden of evidence to the Government. Upholds coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: VELASCO, J.: Martial law is the law of necessity, akin to self-defense; probable cause is the measure, judged on facts presented to the President at the time; later-discovered falsity does not invalidate the act at inception. Quotes Bernas's amicus brief in Fortun that public safety adds a forward-looking nuance to rebellion. Necessity also limits martial law powers (J. Teehankee): intrusions must be proportional, and officers are personally liable for ultra vires acts, the "ultimate safeguard"; discusses warrantless arrests, custodial rights, and IHL.

paras.html: LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.: Concurs on grounds deviating in part from the majority: a certiorari or prohibition petition is not barred as a vehicle (the Fortun opinions tacitly admitted it); "probable cause," "reasonableness," and absence of arbitrariness are practically the same standard, and what matters is how it is applied (J. Muñoz Palma in Aquino v. Ponce Enrile); the Court may relax the burden-of-proof rules, as its closed-door briefing was "judicial activism consistent with" Sec. 18. ISIS-linked groups' unification under an emir justified coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: JARDELEZA, J.: Sufficiency of factual basis is distinct from grave abuse. Proposes a standard of reasonableness ("such evidence that is adequate to satisfy a reasonable mind") because probable cause, a criminal-process standard, cannot measure public safety. As a sui generis proceeding, the Court cannot indulge the presumption of regularity; the Government should first present its facts, and attaching declassified proof to the Report is advisable. Finds public safety reasonably required martial law in all Mindanao (Hapilon as emir, the wilayat plan, the Davao attack).

paras.html: PERLAS-BERNABE, J. (concurring in the result): The proceeding is sui generis (closer to a special proceeding than an action); "sufficient factual basis" means adequate proof, rejecting both probable cause and the Lansang arbitrariness test. The Government bears the burden of proving compliance; executive information enjoys a presumption of regularity as to facts only, not conclusions of law, so the petitioner carries the burden of evidence to debunk it. The Court must ask whether the territorial extent is rationally commensurate to the exigencies; here it was.

paras.html: Sufficiency, not accuracy: Sec. 18, Art. VII requires the Court to determine only the sufficiency of the factual basis, not its accuracy, which is a higher standard. The Court looks at the totality of the facts in the President's possession prior to and at the time of the declaration; subsequent events have no bearing, and inaccuracies in some facts do not invalidate the declaration as long as other facts support the existence of actual rebellion or invasion and the public-safety requirement.
paras.text: Sufficiency, not accuracy: Sec. 18, Art. VII requires the Court to determine only the sufficiency of the factual basis, not its accuracy, which is a higher standard. The Court looks at the totality of the facts in the President's possession prior to and at the time of the declaration; subsequent events have no bearing, and inaccuracies in some facts do not invalidate the declaration as long as other facts support the existence of actual rebellion or invasion and the public-safety requirement.

paras.html: Martial law has a "time fuse": The President's declaration lasts at most 60 days and automatically terminates. Its extension, though initiated by the President, is approved by Congress and is a distinct and separate joint executive-legislative act (RBH No. 11). The expiry of Proclamation No. 216 rendered the challenge to its sufficiency moot, and the Court has no jurisdiction to review the extension in petitions that assail only the proclamation.

paras.html: Leeway is not surrender: The leeway given to the Executive does not concede the judicial power to review; it rests on the requirement of actual (not imminent) rebellion or invasion, which makes time of the essence, and on the President's access to confidential information.

paras.html: Territorial scope is fixed by the Constitution. Sec. 18 requires (1) actual rebellion or invasion and (2) public safety. Actual rebellion, as defined by the RPC (public uprising and taking up arms, with the purpose of removing territory or forces from allegiance or depriving the Chief Executive or Congress of powers; Ladlad v. Velasco), must exist in the particular territory before martial law may be declared there.

paras.html: History. The Jones Law (1916), the 1935 Constitution, and the 1973 Constitution allowed martial law for rebellion "or imminent danger thereof" → placing the whole country under martial law for a local rebellion was then justified by the danger of spread. The 1987 Constitution intentionally removed "imminent danger."

paras.html: Spill-over = imminent danger. Upholding martial law outside Marawi because of a possible "spill-over of hostilities" or escape of rebels would unlawfully reinstate the deleted ground. The President may choose between calling out the armed forces and declaring martial law, but has no wide leeway on territorial scope.

paras.html: Sec. 18 is a neutral, straightforward fact-checking mechanism. It does not assign blame or ascribe grave abuse, so a finding of insufficiency exposes the Executive to no liability.

paras.html: Accuracy is inextricably linked to sufficiency. Sufficient factual basis necessarily means "sufficient truthful, accurate, or at the very least, credible" basis. The Court's judgment is not temporally bound to the date of the proclamation: per the Bernas–Bengzon exchange in the ConCom, the Court's judgment is "transitory" because facts change → the Court may nullify if the facts are shown false or no longer obtaining during review (or uphold if facts later become sufficient).

paras.html: "False dichotomy." Evidence is the means of ascertaining the truth (Rule 128, Sec. 1); accepting false facts makes the quantum of evidence illusory. The Executive's superior data-gathering apparatus should raise the bar, not lower it; otherwise the finding rests on bare allegations, akin to relying on presumptions of regularity, which amounts to judicial rubber-stamping.

paras.html: Congress may extend more than once, for the period it fixes: "Section 18, Article VII is clear that the only limitations to the exercise of the congressional authority to extend such proclamation or suspension are that the extension should be upon the President's initiative; that it should be grounded on the persistence of the invasion or rebellion and the demands of public safety; and that it is subject to the Court's review of the sufficiency of its factual basis upon the petition of any citizen." The "same manner" clause refers to the mode of voting, not to a 60-day period.
paras.text: Congress may extend more than once, for the period it fixes: "Section 18, Article VII is clear that the only limitations to the exercise of the congressional authority to extend such proclamation or suspension are that the extension should be upon the President's initiative; that it should be grounded on the persistence of the invasion or rebellion and the demands of public safety; and that it is subject to the Court's review of the sufficiency of its factual basis upon the petition of any citizen." The "same manner" clause refers to the mode of voting, not to a 60-day period.

paras.html: Scope of the Court's review: Under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII, the Court's review of Congress' extension is limited to the sufficiency of the factual basis; a certiorari petition invoking expanded jurisdiction (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) is not the proper remedy. Because the Court's judgment is "transitory," a ruling on the original proclamation does not bar review of the persistence of the rebellion.
paras.text: Scope of the Court's review: Under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII, the Court's review of Congress' extension is limited to the sufficiency of the factual basis; a certiorari petition invoking expanded jurisdiction (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) is not the proper remedy. Because the Court's judgment is "transitory," a ruling on the original proclamation does not bar review of the persistence of the rebellion.

paras.html: Persistence of rebellion and public safety: Rebellion is a continuing crime; the end of armed combat in one place does not end it, nor does it cease "by estoppel" on account of official pronouncements. Public safety requires the extension when present and past acts of the actual rebellion "endanger and will endanger public safety"; the Constitution sets no threshold that government must first be unable to function.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for not more than 60 days, to address the rebellion of the Maute Group and the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG).

paras.html: May 25, 2017: Within the 48-hour period, the President submitted his written Report to Congress. The Senate (P.S. Res. No. 388) and the House (H. Res. No. 1050) expressed full support and found no cause to revoke.

Rebellion is a continuing crime; members who evaded capture did not cease to be rebels.

paras.html: Including the NPA "will not render it void." The NPA (communist rule) and the DAESH/ISIS-inspired rebels differ in ideology but share the purpose of overthrowing the duly constituted government, and the NPA's violence hardly distinguishes it from the architects of the Marawi siege.

paras.html: The NPA was not included in Proc. 216 because of ongoing peace negotiations ("not explicitly included" as a matter of comity, per the OSG). The NPA intensified offensives despite the talks, prompting their termination (Proc. No. 360) and terrorist designation (Proc. No. 374). It would make no sense to exclude a communist rebellion that persists in the same region.

paras.html: Reliance on the Executive's facts: the President may rely on intelligence reports and classified documents (Lagman). The request was based on AFP and PNP assessments, a "careful personal evaluation" of reports (ES Medialdea), and the President's personal knowledge. The AFP briefed both Houses on December 12; resource persons answered interpellations at the joint session; Rep. Papandayan confirmed remnants' recruitment in Lanao del Sur. Since the facts are with the Executive, "the Court will have to rely on the fact-finding capabilities of the [E]xecutive [D]epartment; in turn, the Executive Department will have to open its findings to the scrutiny of the Court." It did so at oral arguments, with NICA-vetted data whose reliability was not challenged.

paras.html: Martial law is a law of necessity ("Necessity creates the conditions for martial law and at the same time limits the scope of martial law"). When the need ends, the President may lift it before the year ends, and Congress may pre-terminate the extension, since the power to fix the period includes the power to shorten it. Because the Court's judgment is transitory, any citizen may again petition for review if they fail to lift it.

paras.html: The doctrine of necessity: The ponencia sets no parameters for either requirement and no limits on the length or number of extensions. Tracing American cases (Luther v. Borden, Ex parte Milligan, Moyer v. Peabody, Sterling v. Constantin, Duncan v. Kahanamoku), martial law is "the law of necessity in national emergency"; under the 1987 Constitution, necessity is expressed in "public safety requires it."

Borden, Ex parte Milligan, Moyer v. Peabody, Sterling v. Constantin, Duncan v. Kahanamoku), martial law is "the law of necessity in national emergency"; under the 1987 Constitution, necessity is expressed in "public safety requires it."

paras.html: Calibration and proportionality: Following Sterling, the Court must weigh the gravity of the situation against martial law; the danger must arise in a state of significant armed conflict. The Court must also calibrate the territorial coverage and, for extensions, whether the danger is commensurate with the period (as in Lansang v. Garcia).

paras.html: No operational necessity shown: Her exchange with Gen. Guerrero yielded only that martial law is partly "psychological," projects "a strong authority," and eases coordination, an "undocumented experiential claim" against documented claims of abuses.

BIFF and ASG incidents lacked particularity and may have been counted before. The NPA rebellion was not a basis of Proc. 216 as reviewed in Lagman; adding a new actor to show that rebellion "persists" is "self-contradictory."

paras.html: Preliminary: Rejects petitioners' reliance on Ex parte Milligan (martial law as military jurisdiction over civilians in a theater of war); it conflicts with Sec. 18(4), Art. VII, under which the Constitution and civil courts continue to operate.

paras.html: First, the Maute rebellion ceased. "Persist" means the continued existence of the same rebellion cited in the initial proclamation. Proc. 216 and the Report identified the Maute Group. The President's October 17, 2017 declaration of Marawi's liberation, Sec. Lorenzana's announcement ending combat operations, and Col. Brawner's statement confirm that actual rebellion no longer persisted; no evidence of Maute rebellion elsewhere.

Brawner's statement confirm that actual rebellion no longer persisted; no evidence of Maute rebellion elsewhere.

paras.html: Second, remnants' capability is not rebellion. "Capability to rebel, absent an actual rebellion or invasion, is not a ground"; allowing it would reinstate "imminent danger," which was intentionally removed.

paras.html: Third, the NPA rebellion cannot justify the extension. Lagman upheld Proc. 216 solely on the Maute rebellion. Citing the NPA bypasses the mandatory 60-day period for an initial declaration; the government may proclaim martial law over the NPA rebellion, but must observe the 60 days before seeking extension. Congress' concurrence cannot cure this.

paras.html: A rebellion "survives in legal existence" until the movement stops; a showing of substantial inactivity or loss of capability suffices to end it. No such showing here; rebels regrouped. Supervening activities of other groups (BIFF, Turaifie, NPA) may be considered; nothing requires an extension to relate solely to the same group. Public safety is a more malleable concept deserving deference, circumscribed by truth and reason.

paras.html: Heightened scrutiny: Sec. 18 requires stricter review than past Constitutions (tracing Barcelon, Montenegro, Lansang, Aquino v. Enrile, Parong) and includes review for grave abuse. The majority's deferential review is "a reincarnation of the political question doctrine."

paras.html: Undefined powers and targets: There can be no rational review when the powers to be exercised under martial law are not defined; the request was a "carte blanche." The government gave no targets beyond "to quell the rebellion," and Gen. Guerrero cited mainly a "psychological advantage." Rehabilitation and economic goals are not grounds.

paras.html: Evidence: Letters and briefings are allegations (factum probandum versus factum probans); intelligence must be shown to have undergone rigorous analysis. Recruitment motives (clan, revenge, money) do not show rebellion; 537 rebels against more than 100,000 AFP personnel; no basis for covering all of Mindanao; no basis for one year.

paras.html: NPA and terrorism: The NPA's "surreptitious insertion" was not a basis of Proc. 216; its attacks targeted private entities. Terrorism differs from rebellion and calls for counter-violent-extremism programs (citing the UK's CONTEST), not military rule.

paras.html: Pardon does not ipso facto restore a forfeited public office: An absolute pardon granted after conviction frees the individual from all the penalties and legal disabilities and restores his civil rights, and it restores his eligibility for appointment to the office forfeited by the conviction. But it does not ipso facto restore him to that office; he must reapply and undergo the usual procedure for a new appointment, and the appointing power may weigh the facts of the offense.
paras.text: Pardon does not ipso facto restore a forfeited public office: An absolute pardon granted after conviction frees the individual from all the penalties and legal disabilities and restores his civil rights, and it restores his eligibility for appointment to the office forfeited by the conviction. But it does not ipso facto restore him to that office; he must reapply and undergo the usual procedure for a new appointment, and the appointing power may weigh the facts of the offense.

paras.html: Pardon implies guilt: "Pardon implies guilt. It does not erase the fact of the commission of the crime and the conviction thereof. It does not wash out the moral stain. It involves forgiveness and not forgetfulness." Unless expressly grounded on innocence, it cannot restore lost reputation. It looks to the future and is not retrospective, so it gives no right to backpay.

paras.html: Definition (United States v. Wilson): "an act of grace, proceeding from the power entrusted with the execution of the laws, which exempts the individual, on whom it is bestowed, from the punishment the law inflicts for a crime he has committed." It is a private, though official, act of the executive, not communicated officially to the Court. A pardon is a deed, to the validity of which delivery is essential, and delivery is not complete without acceptance.

Labrador (1940): subject to constitutional limits, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action; an absolute pardon "not only blots out the crime committed but removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction"; the Chief Executive should be at liberty to relieve the party completely "from the accessory and resultant disabilities of criminal conviction."

paras.html: These cases and others (In re Lontok, Pendon v. Diasnes, Mijares v. Custorio) show the unmistakable application of the doctrinal case of Ex parte Garland, whose "sweeping generalizations" still hold sway here even though later American decisions downplayed much of its relevance.

paras.html: The Court's "vital point": the Court concedes that pardon may remit all the penal consequences of a criminal indictment, to give meaning to the principle that a pardon, being a presidential prerogative, should not be circumscribed by legislative action. But it rejects the "fictitious belief" that pardon blots out guilt and that the pardoned person must be treated as innocent; pardon cannot produce such "moral changes" as to equate a pardoned convict with a constantly law-abiding citizen.

paras.html: No military trial of civilians while civil courts function: A military commission or tribunal cannot try and exercise jurisdiction, even during the period of martial law, over civilians for offenses allegedly committed by them as long as the civil courts are open and functioning, and any judgment it renders relating to a civilian is null and void for lack of jurisdiction. Aquino, Jr. v. Military Commission No. 2 (1975) and the cases affirming it are abandoned insofar as inconsistent.

paras.text: Lifting of martial law:

paras.html: On January 17, 1981, President Marcos issued Proclamation No. 2045, officially lifting martial law. It revoked General Order No. 8 (which created the military tribunals) and directed that the military tribunals "are hereby dissolved upon final determination of cases pending therein which may not be transferred to the civil courts without irreparable prejudice to the state in view of the rules on double jeopardy, or other circumstances which render prosecution of the cases difficult, if not impossible."

paras.html: Due process demands that in all criminal prosecutions (where the accused stands to lose life or liberty), the accused is entitled to, among others, a trial (In re Oliver; Secs. 1 and 14(2), Art. III, 1987 Constitution).

paras.html: Civilians placed on trial for civil offenses under general law are entitled to trial by judicial process. Judicial power is vested by the Constitution exclusively in the SC and in inferior courts established by law, which have "exclusive power to hear and determine those matters which affect the life or liberty or property of a citizen" (citing Lopez v. Roxas; Scoty's Department Store v. Micaller).

paras.html: "Since we are not enemy-occupied territory nor are we under a military government and even on the premise that martial law continues in force," military tribunals cannot try civilians for civil offenses cognizable by civil courts that have remained open and regularly functioning (citing Ex parte Milligan).

paras.html: Toth v. Quarles (U.S.): "the assertion of military authority over civilians cannot rest on the President's power as Commander-in-Chief or on any theory of martial law." The presiding officer of a court-martial is not a judge protected by tenure and undiminished salary; different rules of evidence and procedure apply; and the convening officer, who selects members and counsel and commands them, can influence the outcome.

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the Petitions for habeas corpus are DISMISSED for having become moot and academic. The Petitions for certiorari and prohibition are hereby GRANTED. The creation of respondent Military Commission No. 34 to try civilians like the petitioners is hereby declared unconstitutional and all its proceedings are deemed null and void. The temporary restraining order enjoining respondents from executing the Decision of MC 34 is made permanent, and respondents are permanently prohibited from further pursuing Criminal Case No. MC-34-1 against petitioners. The sentence imposing the death penalty on petitioners is vacated for being null and void, and all items or properties taken from petitioners in relation to the case shall be returned to them immediately. No pronouncement as to costs.

paras.html: Apart from the right to trial by judicial process, petitioners were denied an impartial trial from the start: the President (Commander-in-Chief) and the Defense Minister, the supposed targets of the conspiracy, were the very authorities who approved the charges and referred them to MC 34.

paras.html: As reviewing authorities, they could reverse or modify any judgment, even an acquittal, and could substitute commission members at pleasure, assign them to hazardous duties, and promote them or block their promotion. Members could hardly go against their superiors' declaration of "overwhelming" evidence.

paras.html: Quotes his own Aquino, Jr. dissent: Marcos publicly declared the evidence against Aquino "not only strong (but) overwhelming" at the August 24, 1971 press conference after the Plaza Miranda bombing; due process requires "the cold neutrality of an independent, wholly free, disinterested and impartial tribunal." Marcos himself had said that "if it were not for the judicial process, I would not be President," yet denied Aquino that process.

paras.html: Hails the reinstatement of the rule, "greatly eroded" under martial law, that disregard of an accused's constitutional rights ousts the tribunal of jurisdiction, and habeas corpus is the appropriate remedy (Gumabon). paras.html: 4. Sec. 18, Art. VII, 1987 Constitution – checks on martial law
paras.text: 4. Sec. 18, Art. VII, 1987 Constitution – checks on martial law

paras.html: Lists the changes summarized by former C.J. Roberto Concepcion in his last public address, including: martial law does not suspend the Constitution, supplant civil courts, or confer jurisdiction on military courts over civilians where civil courts function; it does not automatically suspend the privilege of the writ; it cannot be declared on mere imminent danger; the President must report to Congress within 48 hours; Congress may revoke by a majority vote of all its members, which the President cannot set aside; it may not exceed 60 days without Congress's concurrence; the SC may review the sufficiency of its factual basis in a proceeding filed by any citizen and must decide within 30 days; a simple majority now suffices to declare a law unconstitutional; and a detainee must be released unless judicially charged within three days.

paras.html: No automatic joint session: “The Congress is not constitutionally mandated to convene in joint session except to vote jointly to revoke the President's declaration or suspension.” The phrase “voting jointly” in Art. VII, Sec. 18 explicitly applies only to revocation. But if either House, or both, resolves to revoke, Congress must convene in joint session to vote jointly on the revocation.
paras.text: No automatic joint session: “The Congress is not constitutionally mandated to convene in joint session except to vote jointly to revoke the President's declaration or suspension.” The phrase “voting jointly” in Art. VII, Sec. 18 explicitly applies only to revocation. But if either House, or both, resolves to revoke, Congress must convene in joint session to vote jointly on the revocation.

paras.html: Concurrence is left to each House: The Constitution does not provide for the manner by which Congress expresses concurrence (prior or subsequent) in a proclamation or suspension; the Houses have the discretion to adopt rules of procedure for that purpose (Art. VI, Sec. 16[3]). This does not place the rules of the Houses above the Constitution.

paras.html: May 23, 2017 – President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring a state of martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for a period not exceeding 60 days, on the grounds of rebellion and the necessity of public safety under Art. VII, Sec. 18.
paras.text: May 23, 2017 – President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring a state of martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for a period not exceeding 60 days, on the grounds of rebellion and the necessity of public safety under Art. VII, Sec. 18.

paras.html: Basis (per the Proclamation and the Report): a series of armed attacks and atrocities by the Abu Sayyaf and Maute terrorist groups, with local and foreign affiliates who pledged allegiance to ISIS, aimed at establishing a DAESH wilayah (Islamic Province) in Mindanao.

paras.html: May 31, 2017 – The Committee of the Whole was briefed in a closed-door session (about 6 hours) by ES Medialdea, Sec. Lorenzana, and other security officials. A proposal to call a joint session was debated and rejected.

paras.html: No standing: Generalized interests do not confer standing; petitioners show no direct and personal interest. A taxpayer's suit lies only against the exercise of the spending or taxing power, and martial law is being funded from funds already appropriated. Sen. De Lima suffers no prejudice where Congress's powers are not impaired; and even assuming they were, she has not shown she has been allowed to participate in Senate sessions during her incarceration, so she has no direct injury.

paras.html: Citizens: Every citizen has the right, if not the duty, to see that a public grievance is remedied (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo). A citizen asserting a public right represents the public at large; it is enough that he shows he is entitled to relief in the vindication of a public right (De Castro v. JBC). His personal interest lies in being a member of the public in whom the right is vested (Legaspi v. CSC) and in his interest and duty to ensure the proper execution of the law (Tañada v. Tuvera).

paras.html: Plain text: Art. VII, Sec. 18 requires Congress to convene in joint session, deliberate, and vote as a single deliberative body; this is mandatory, not discretionary.
paras.text: Plain text: Art. VII, Sec. 18 requires Congress to convene in joint session, deliberate, and vote as a single deliberative body; this is mandatory, not discretionary.

paras.html: “May” qualifies only the power to revoke, not the obligation to convene jointly and vote. Requiring a joint session only when Congress will revoke is absurd, because without convening jointly, Congress cannot know beforehand whether a majority for revocation exists.

paras.html: Framers' intent: The joint session was designed to compel Congress to review the President's action and to contain martial law within a democratic framework. The Tañada petitioners add that “voting jointly” was meant as a procedural requirement for Congress to revoke, affirm, or extend, whether or not Congress is in session or intends to revoke.

paras.html: Fortun v. Macapagal-Arroyo described Congress's duty to convene jointly as “automatic.” The 2009 Maguindanao joint session is a legislative precedent.

paras.html: 24-hour clause: If Congress not in session must convene within 24 hours, then all the more must it convene immediately when in session.
paras.text: 24-hour clause: If Congress not in session must convene within 24 hours, then all the more must it convene immediately when in session.

paras.html: Deliberation, transparency, accountability: Separate briefings in executive sessions deprive lawmakers of a deliberative and interrogatory process and the public of transparent proceedings; legislators who wish to revoke should be able to put that vote on record, and the public should know each legislator's position. A regular session is preferable to a briefing so that officials testify under oath.

paras.html: There is no mandatory duty to “vote jointly” except to revoke or extend. Sec. 18 does not use the words “joint session” at all.

paras.html: Prior concurrence of Congress is not required for the effectivity of the proclamation; the framers intended to let the President act for up to 60 days without it. Nothing mandates a joint session merely to discuss or review the proclamation. When Congress is not in session, it convenes “in accordance with its rules,” not in joint session.

To guard against abuse, Sec. 18 institutionalized checks through Congress (report; revoke; extend) and the Judiciary (sufficiency of factual basis).

paras.html: Four provisions concern Congress: (a) the 48-hour report; (b) revocation by joint vote; (c) extension on the President's initiative “in the same manner”; and (d) convening within 24 hours if not in session.
