paras.html: Plain-meaning rule: when the law is clear, there is no room for construction, only application (Bolos v. Bolos); applied to the Constitution in Funa v. Villar, citing J.M. Tuason v. LTA (words given their ordinary meaning; “the framers and the people mean what they say”).

paras.html: The provision is clear, plain, and unambiguous: it grants Congress the power to revoke and prescribes how — a majority of all Members, voting jointly, in regular or special session.

paras.html: “May” is permissive and confers discretion on whether to revoke (Ombudsman v. De Sahagun); but to revoke, a joint-vote majority is required.

VI, Sec. 23(1) — “joint session assembled, voting separately” — and Art. VII, Sec. 4 — “joint public session”).

ES: intent is a “foolproof yardstick,” but debates may be consulted only when other guides fail; they are powerless to vary clear terms, and it is “safer to construe the constitution from what appears upon its face.” → Since the text is clear, there is no need to look further; nonetheless, the deliberations show no manifest intent to require a joint session in all cases. They show two intentions:
paras.text: Civil Liberties Union v. ES: intent is a “foolproof yardstick,” but debates may be consulted only when other guides fail; they are powerless to vary clear terms, and it is “safer to construe the constitution from what appears upon its face.” → Since the text is clear, there is no need to look further; nonetheless, the deliberations show no manifest intent to require a joint session in all cases. They show two intentions:

paras.html: (a) Remove prior concurrence. The draft required the concurrence of a majority of all Members for the suspension. Natividad, Padilla, and Monsod argued that in actual invasion or rebellion the President must act fast, concurrence may be impractical, the proclamation has a 60-day “time fuse,” and the SC can review the factual basis; Suarez warned of another Marcos. Vote: 28–12 to delete prior concurrence.

Vote: 28–12 to delete prior concurrence.

paras.html: (b) Discretionary power to revoke by joint vote. The debate was whether the Houses vote jointly or separately — always for the purpose of revocation. Bernas proposed joint voting as a conscious exception so that it is easier for Congress to revoke and to avoid a deadlock; Monsod agreed (Senators would participate in discussions and lend persuasive weight); Rodrigo and Ople objected that the Senate would be absorbed by the House. Vote: 24–13 for “voting jointly.”

paras.html: Rodrigo's later amendment to give the power to the House alone was rejected 5–25. Rodrigo expressly observed that the provision “does not call for a joint session.”

paras.html: The Commissioners settled only the manner of voting to revoke; they did not specify that voting be done in a joint session. A joint session can only be inferred from the argument that Representatives would benefit from the Senators' advice → “far from a clear mandate” to automatically convene jointly under all circumstances, even when Congress does not intend to revoke.

paras.html: Result: The Constitution does not provide at all for the manner of concurrence (prior or subsequent). Here, both Houses separately passed resolutions of support under their own rules. By contrast, it explicitly provides how Congress may revoke.

paras.html: Both Houses adopted resolutions supporting Proclamation No. 216 and showed no intent to revoke → the provision on revocation “did not even come into operation” → no obligation to convene jointly.

paras.html: “Practice and logic dictate” that a collegial body first meets among its own members to reach a stance before convening with another body — exactly what the Houses did. Each House took prompt action: received and assessed the Report, interpellated executive officials, deliberated, then voted to support the proclamation and against a joint session. They placed the proclamation under serious review.

paras.html: By practice, a joint session requires a concurrent resolution; the Houses then adopt ad hoc rules for that session (e.g., 2016 canvass rules; 2009 rules on Proclamation No. 1959), which become functus officio once the purpose is achieved. No concurrent resolution was adopted → no joint session could be had.

paras.html: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3) (“Each House shall determine the rules of its proceedings”) is a grant of full discretionary authority generally exempt from judicial interference (Dela Paz v. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations); legislative acts following long-settled practice carry an “armor of constitutionality” (McGillicuddy, a U.S. state case). Qualifier: “Nothing in this Decision should be presumed to give precedence to the rules of the Houses of the Congress over the provisions of the Constitution.” The Court holds only that, since the Constitution does not regulate the manner of concurrence, the Houses may adopt rules for it.

paras.html: The pardoning power cannot be limited by legislative action: The only instances in which the President may not extend pardon are (1) impeachment cases, (2) cases without a final conviction, and (3) violations of election laws, rules, and regulations without the COMELEC's favorable recommendation (Sec. 19, Art. VII; Sec. 5, Art. IX-C). "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

VII; Sec. 5, Art. IX-C). "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 of the RPC are harmonized, not applied rigidly: They only impart that the pardon of the principal penalty does not carry the remission of the accessory penalties unless the President expressly includes them. A pardon stating that the grantee "is hereby restored to his civil and political rights" substantially complies with the requirement of express restoration, because the right to seek public elective office is a political right.

paras.html: A whereas clause cannot make a pardon conditional: A preamble is not part of the operative language; absent a condition stated in the pardon itself, a "whereas" recital does not limit its scope or make its effectivity contingent.

paras.html: On September 12, 2007, the Sandiganbayan convicted former President Joseph Ejercito Estrada of plunder (Crim. Case No. 26558; RA 7080, as amended by RA 7659). Finding no aggravating or mitigating circumstance, it imposed the lesser penalty under Art. 63 RPC: reclusion perpetua with the accessory penalties of civil interdiction during the period of sentence and perpetual absolute disqualification. It also declared forfeited the Erap Muslim Youth Foundation deposit, the Jose Velarde account (₱189,000,000.00), and the "Boracay Mansion." [sic: the first forfeited amount reads "Five Hundred Forty-Two Million Seven Hundred Ninety-One Thousand Pesos (P545,291,000.00)"; the publisher notes the discrepancy between words and figures.]

paras.html: On November 30, 2009, Estrada filed a COC for President. Three oppositions were filed with the COMELEC: (1) SPA No. 09-024 (DC), a petition to deny due course to and cancel his COC, by Rev. Elly Velez B. Lao Pamatong; (2) SPA No. 09-028 (DC), a petition for disqualification, by Atty. Evilio C. Pormento; and (3) SPA No. 09-104 (DC), a petition to disqualify, by Mary Lou Estrada.

paras.html: In separate Resolutions dated January 20, 2010, the COMELEC Second Division effectively dismissed all three on uniform grounds: (i) the constitutional proscription on reelection applies to a sitting president; and (ii) the pardon restored Estrada's right to vote and be voted for a public office. The COMELEC En Banc denied the motions for reconsideration.

paras.text: On January 24, 2013 [Leonen's dissent gives January 14, 2013 as the filing date and January 24, 2013 as the date of Estrada's answer], Risos-Vidal filed a petition for disqualification with the COMELEC (SPA No. 13-211 (DC)). She argued that Estrada is disqualified because of his plunder conviction and his sentence of reclusion perpetua with perpetual absolute disqualification, relying on Sec. 40 of the LGC in relation to Sec. 12 of the OEC:

paras.html: Sec. 40, LGC. The following persons are disqualified from running for any elective local position: (a) Those sentenced by final judgment for an offense involving moral turpitude or for an offense punishable by one (1) year or more of imprisonment, within two (2) years after serving sentence; …
paras.text: Sec. 40, LGC. The following persons are disqualified from running for any elective local position: (a) Those sentenced by final judgment for an offense involving moral turpitude or for an offense punishable by one (1) year or more of imprisonment, within two (2) years after serving sentence; …

paras.html: Sec. 12, OEC. Any person who … has been sentenced by final judgment … for any offense for which he has been sentenced to a penalty of more than eighteen months or for a crime involving moral turpitude, shall be disqualified to be a candidate and to hold any public office, unless he has been given plenary pardon or granted amnesty.
paras.text: Sec. 12, OEC. Any person who … has been sentenced by final judgment … for any offense for which he has been sentenced to a penalty of more than eighteen months or for a crime involving moral turpitude, shall be disqualified to be a candidate and to hold any public office, unless he has been given plenary pardon or granted amnesty.

paras.html: On April 1, 2013, the COMELEC Second Division dismissed the petition "for utter lack of merit." Having taken judicial cognizance of the consolidated 2010 resolution in SPA Nos. 09-028 and 09-104 and the En Banc resolution affirming it, it would "not belabor the controversy further"; Risos-Vidal failed to present cogent proof to reverse its standing pronouncement that the pardon restored Estrada's right to seek public office, and it would "no longer engage in disquisitions of a settled matter."

paras.html: On April 30, 2013, Risos-Vidal filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64, in relation to Rule 65, to annul the two COMELEC Resolutions for grave abuse of discretion. She raised five issues: the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion (I) in holding that the pardon was not conditional; (II) in not finding Estrada disqualified under Sec. 40 LGC for plunder, a crime involving moral turpitude; (III) in dismissing her petition because it involved the same issues resolved in the 2010 Pormento and Mary Lou Estrada cases; (IV) in not ruling that the pardon neither restored his right of suffrage nor remitted his perpetual absolute disqualification; and (V) in not disqualifying him motu proprio.

paras.html: The pardon was conditional. Estrada's express acceptance shows its conditional nature, and the condition is the third whereas clause (his public commitment to no longer seek elective office). That commitment impelled PGMA to grant the pardon; by filing COCs for President and for Mayor, he breached it, so "he ought to be recommitted to prison to serve the unexpired portion of his sentence" and is disqualified.

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 RPC are mandatory. A general restoration of "civil and political rights" does not restore the right to hold public office or the right of suffrage, nor remit civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification, unless the specific rights are categorically mentioned. They shun a general or implied restoration.

paras.html: Monsanto v. Factoran, Jr. Citing the concurring opinions of JJ. Padilla and Feliciano, restoration of the right to hold public office "cannot be left to inference, no matter how intensely arguable, but must be stated in express, explicit, positive and specific language." Express restoration is further demanded by the third whereas clause.

paras.html: The codal provisions must be construed to harmonize the power of Congress to define crimes and prescribe penalties with the President's power to grant clemency. "All that the said provisions impart is that the pardon of the principal penalty does not carry with it the remission of the accessory penalties unless the President expressly includes said accessory penalties in the pardon." They still recognize the President's choice to pardon the principal penalty alone or both; they "only clarify the effect of the pardon."

paras.html: Applied (even under Arts. 36 and 41): The pardon's first sentence covers the principal penalty of reclusion perpetua (relieving imprisonment); the second sentence, "He is hereby restored to his civil and political rights," expressly remitted the accessory penalties. "Hence, even if we apply Articles 36 and 41 … it is indubitable from the text of the pardon that the accessory penalties of civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification were expressly remitted."

paras.html: A preamble "is not an essential part of an act"; it merely explains the reasons for it (People v. Balasa), and whereas clauses are not part of the operative language (Llamado v. CA). The clause "is not an integral part of the decree of the pardon" and does not by itself make the pardon conditional, make its effectivity contingent on the commitment, or limit its scope.

paras.html: Ponencia: [sic: the ponencia here lapses into the first person, "With due respect, I disagree."] It rejects "the overbroad statement that Congress may dictate as to how the President may exercise his/her power of executive clemency." paras.html: No res judicata: The 2010 cases rested on the reelection ban (Sec. 4, Art. VII) and the nuisance-candidate ground, not on Sec. 40 LGC; the subject matter differed (presidency v. mayoralty); the COMELEC's pardon statements were obiter; and Pormento ended in mootness, so there was no final judgment on the merits.

paras.html: Nature of pardon: "Forgiveness but not forgetfulness." Monsanto repudiated Garland, Cristobal, and Pelobello; pardon is a private, though official, act that does not erase the moral stain.
paras.text: Nature of pardon: "Forgiveness but not forgetfulness." Monsanto repudiated Garland, Cristobal, and Pelobello; pardon is a private, though official, act that does not erase the moral stain.

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 do not abridge the pardoning power: They do not reduce its coverage (Llamas v. Orbos); they are "requirements of convention or form" asking the President to state the intent "clearly, directly, firmly, precisely, and unmistakably." Public office is a public trust, while pardon is a private act; the phrase "as otherwise provided in this Constitution" requires reading Sec. 19 with the public-trust injunction.

Public office is a public trust, while pardon is a private act; the phrase "as otherwise provided in this Constitution" requires reading Sec. 19 with the public-trust injunction.

paras.html: Clarifying Monsanto: Its "inclusion" statement was made in a comparative survey, relied on a U.S. case, and did not account for Arts. 36 and 41; it is superseded by People v. Casido and People v. Patriarca (citing Barrioquinto v. Fernandez) and Romeo Jalosjos v. COMELEC (2013).
paras.text: Clarifying Monsanto: Its "inclusion" statement was made in a comparative survey, relied on a U.S. case, and did not account for Arts. 36 and 41; it is superseded by People v. Casido and People v. Patriarca (citing Barrioquinto v. Fernandez) and Romeo Jalosjos v. COMELEC (2013).

paras.html: No express restoration or remission: The pardon is silent on suffrage, office, and perpetual absolute disqualification. Estrada relies on inference ("deemed subsumed," "substantial compliance"), which is exactly what "express" excludes. "Civil and political rights" is a collectivity or "basket" (ICCPR; Vasak; Simon v. CHR), while Arts. 36 and 41 single out suffrage and office. PGMA departed from the standard "full civil and political rights" formula and was silent; together these mean the rights were not restored. Estrada's other civil and political rights were restored.

paras.html: Preambular clauses: Even if ambiguous, the whereas clauses resolve it against Estrada (People v. Purisima). The third clause is "an indispensable qualifier": the pardon was premised on his promise not to seek office, consistent with the gravity of plunder (Estrada v. Sandiganbayan: malum in se).

paras.html: A declaration of a state of rebellion is valid but legally superfluous: The President's authority to declare a state of rebellion "springs in the main from her powers as chief executive and, at the same time, draws strength from her Commander-in-Chief powers" (with statutory basis in Sec. 4, Ch. 2, Bk. III, Administrative Code of 1987). But in calling out the armed forces, the declaration is "an utter superfluity": it only gives notice that a rebellion exists, is "devoid of any legal significance," and cannot diminish constitutional rights or by itself justify warrantless arrests.

But in calling out the armed forces, the declaration is "an utter superfluity": it only gives notice that a rebellion exists, is "devoid of any legal significance," and cannot diminish constitutional rights or by itself justify warrantless arrests.

paras.html: Calling-out power needs no declaration: Sec. 18, Art. VII grants graduated powers. Actual invasion or rebellion and public safety are required only for suspending the privilege of the writ and declaring martial law; the calling-out power requires only that it "becomes necessary."

paras.html: Moot but capable of repetition yet evading review; legislators' standing: A moot case may still be decided if it is "capable of repetition yet evading review." Members of Congress have standing when an executive act impairs Congress's powers; organizations, taxpayers and citizens must show direct injury (taxpayers: illegal disbursement of public funds).

paras.html: In the wee hours of July 27, 2003, some three hundred junior officers and enlisted men of the AFP, armed with high-powered ammunitions and explosives, stormed the Oakwood Premiere apartments in Makati City. [The Ynares-Santiago and Sandoval-Gutierrez dissents put the number at 323 and identify them as the "Magdalo Group."]

paras.html: Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4:
paras.text: Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4:

paras.html: Later that day, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (PGMA) issued Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4, both declaring "a state of rebellion" and calling out the AFP (and the PNP) to suppress the rebellion. [Per the dissents, Proc. 427 was issued at about 1:00 p.m.]

paras.html: Proc. 427 recited that certain AFP elements had seized a building in Makati, planted bombs, publicly withdrawn support from the Government, and taken arms against it, acts which "constitute the crime of rebellion punishable under Article 134 of the Revised Penal Code"; it invoked Sec. 18, Art. VII and stated:

VII and stated:

paras.html: "NOW, THEREFORE, I, GLORIA MACAPAGAL-ARROYO, by virtue of the powers vested in me by law, hereby confirm the existence of an actual and on-going rebellion, compelling me to declare a state of rebellion."
paras.text: "NOW, THEREFORE, I, GLORIA MACAPAGAL-ARROYO, by virtue of the powers vested in me by law, hereby confirm the existence of an actual and on-going rebellion, compelling me to declare a state of rebellion."

Executive Secretary): SJS officers/members, suing as "Filipino citizens, taxpayers, law professors and bar reviewers," argue that (a) Sec. 18 does not authorize the declaration; (b) it is a "constitutional anomaly" that "confuses, confounds and misleads," since "[o]verzealous public officers ... are liable to violate the constitutional right of private citizens"; (c) it circumvents the 48-hour report requirement for martial law; and (d) it cannot be an exercise of emergency powers because Congress has delegated none.

paras.html: Legal standing is "a personal and substantial interest in the case such that the party has sustained or will sustain direct injury as a result of the governmental act," i.e., "such personal stake in the outcome of the controversy as to assure that concrete adverseness which sharpens the presentation of issues" (IBP v. Zamora).

paras.html: Andrew Jackson: defeated South Carolina's nullification of the Tariff Acts of 1828 and 1832; in his Dec. 10, 1832 Proclamation he warned that "disunion by armed force is treason."

paras.html: Abraham Lincoln: joined the CinC and executive-power clauses into "the war power"; called for 75,000 troops, suspended the writ, issued the Emancipation Proclamation. In the Prize Cases (1863), the U.S. Supreme Court, 5–4, upheld his blockade without prior congressional declaration of war.

paras.html: Grover Cleveland: sent federal troops to Illinois against striking railway workers who defied an injunction, without the Governor's request; In re Debs upheld Debs's contempt conviction, recognizing the Nation's duty to secure the common rights entrusted to it.

paras.html: Theodore Roosevelt: "stewardship theory": executive power is limited only by specific restrictions in the Constitution or imposed by Congress; planned to seize Pennsylvania's coal mines as CinC during the 1902 strike. The State's power to take over vital utilities in the public interest was later accepted (→ Sec. 6, Art. XIII, 1935; Sec. 7, Art. XIV, 1973; Sec. 18, Art. XII, 1987).

paras.html: If the requisites for a warrantless arrest must still be present anyway, the declaration is a superfluity. She "shudder[s]" at a blanket affirmation of the President's power to issue declarations that may be untrue or may stay in effect after the rebellion has ended.

paras.html: Facts she adds (citing the Feliciano Fact-Finding Commission Report): Proc. 427 was issued at 1:00 p.m. while 323 soldiers occupied Oakwood; searches ran from July 27 to Aug. 1 and found staging points in Cavite, Makati and Mandaluyong; Ramon Cardenas (Asst. Exec. Sec. of the previous administration) was arrested, presented to the media in handcuffs, brought to DOJ inquest on July 28, and charged with rebellion (later allowed bail); on July 31, a DOJ spokesperson said the "indefinite" state of rebellion made warrantless arrests valid; police released "evidence" linking opposition figures (Sen. Honasan; Sen. Loi Ejercito and Mayor JV Ejercito).

paras.html: Factual basis ignored: The majority discussed only the abstract nature of the powers, without considering whether there was a factual basis for the declaration and when it ended → it returns to, if not expands, Garcia-Padilla v. Enrile, which overturned Lansang v. Garcia (judicial inquiry into factual bases). The 1987 Constitution's grave-abuse clause (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) was meant precisely to check executive abuse.

paras.html: The declaration gives the President no extra powers and "does not have any good purpose"; if used to justify warrantless arrests after the rebellion ended (as with Cardenas), the declaration, or at least the arrest, must be struck down.

paras.html: Rebellion and coup d'etat ended with the surrender: Under Arts. 134 and 134-A, RPC, rebellion is committed only by rising publicly and taking up arms, and coup d'etat only by a swift attack; once these cease, the crime is no longer being committed. The "continuing crime" doctrine (Lansang; Umil v. Ramos) should apply only to subversive armed organizations such as the NPA.

paras.html: No valid warrantless arrest after July 27: Under Sec. 5(a) and (b), Rule 113, no crime was being attempted, committed, or "had just been committed" after the surrender → the declaration's purpose and duration only gave "legal cover" for warrantless arrests.

paras.html: I. Facts she adds: The "Magdalo Group" (323 soldiers) aired grievances on graft in the military, sale of arms to "enemies" of the State, the Davao bombings allegedly ordered by ISAFP Chief Gen. Victor Corpus, increased U.S. military assistance, and "micromanagement" by SND Reyes. PGMA set a 5:00 p.m. deadline at 9:00 a.m., issued Proc. 427 and GO 4 at 1:00 p.m., extended the deadline to 7:00 p.m.; the soldiers left at 11:00 p.m. On July 28, the NBI searched Ramon Cardenas's house, and he was charged with rebellion; Mandaluyong police searched Laarni Enriquez's townhouses (alleged staging areas). After the lifting: an Aug. 4 coup d'etat complaint against Sen. Honasan and about 1,000 "John and Jane Does," and an Aug. 8 recommendation to prosecute Enriquez and Romy Escalona for rebellion.

paras.html: II–III. No constitutional power to declare a state of rebellion: Nowhere does the Constitution grant it. Under Sec. 18, the President may only (1) call out the armed forces, (2) suspend the writ, or (3) declare martial law. If the purpose was merely to call out, she could simply have ordered the AFP.

Under Sec. 18, the President may only (1) call out the armed forces, (2) suspend the writ, or (3) declare martial law. If the purpose was merely to call out, she could simply have ordered the AFP.

paras.html: The "unorthodox measure" is unbounded and leaves the people ignorant of their rights. The safeguards for the writ and martial law (public safety; 60 days; 48-hour report; revocation by Congress; SC review of factual basis within 30 days) are absent from a "state of rebellion" → "How can excess of power be curtailed at its inception?"

paras.text: "Extraordinary conditions do not create or enlarge constitutional power."

paras.html: The May 1, 2001 precedent: On the mere declaration, police arrested without warrants Sen. Enrile and Amb. Maceda and hunted Honasan, Lacson and others, none of whom was caught in the act or arrested on personal knowledge → "In effect, she placed the Philippines under martial law without a declaration to that effect"; violates Sec. 2, Art. III and is unjustified even under Sec. 5, Rule 113.

paras.html: Here, the declaration continued until Aug. 1 though the rebellion had ceased; several searches and seizures took place during the extended period.

paras.html: Congress's concurrent power: Emergency powers should be exercised jointly with Congress (Sec. 18 report and revocation; Sec. 23, Art. VI). By declaring a state of rebellion, PGMA disregarded that concurrent power; "the accumulation of both the executive and legislative powers in the same hands constitutes the very definition of tyranny."

paras.html: IV. U.S. cases do not support the majority: Every proposal to confer uncontrollable power on the U.S. President has been rejected. In re Debs was eroded by Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (Steel Seizure Case), quoting Justice Jackson's concurrence [the opinion says "Mr. Justice Andrew Jackson" (sic: Robert H. Jackson)] on "loose and irresponsible use of adjectives" like "inherent" powers; and by United States v. U.S. District Court (rejecting inherent power for warrantless domestic surveillance). The Prize Cases concern foreign affairs, where executive power predominates; in domestic affairs, the executive role is ancillary to Congress.

paras.html: V. In fine: Every presidential claim to power must be scrutinized; enumerated powers do not include undefined powers.

paras.html: Breach of a conditional pardon may be determined by the President alone: Where the President opts to proceed under Sec. 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code, "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court", before the convict may be recommitted for violating his conditional pardon.
paras.text: Breach of a conditional pardon may be determined by the President alone: Where the President opts to proceed under Sec. 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code, "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court", before the convict may be recommitted for violating his conditional pardon.

paras.html: Two options, and the choice is the President's: The Executive may proceed either under Sec. 64(i), RAC (administrative recommitment to serve the remitted portion of the original sentence) or under Art. 159, RPC (prosecution for violation of a conditional pardon). The choice is an exercise of executive prerogative and is not subject to judicial scrutiny. paras.html: Re: The state of the case law (three propositions):
paras.text: Re: The state of the case law (three propositions):

paras.html: (1) The grant of pardon and the determination of the terms and conditions of a conditional pardon are purely executive acts not subject to judicial scrutiny.
paras.text: (1) The grant of pardon and the determination of the terms and conditions of a conditional pardon are purely executive acts not subject to judicial scrutiny.

paras.html: (2) The determination of a breach of a condition, and its proper consequences, may be either (a) a purely executive act under Sec. 64(i), RAC, not subject to judicial scrutiny; or (b) a judicial act, i.e., trial for and conviction of violation of a conditional pardon under Art. 159, RPC. Where the President opts for Sec. 64(i), "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court". [sic: the decision says the convict may be "recommended" for the violation; context indicates "recommitted."]

Where the President opts for Sec. 64(i), "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court". [sic: the decision says the convict may be "recommended" for the violation; context indicates "recommitted."]

paras.html: (3) Because due process is not "semper et ubique" judicial process, and the convict was already accorded judicial due process for the original offense, Sec. 64(i) is not afflicted with a constitutional vice.

paras.text: The petitioner was a convict "who had already been seized in a constitutional way, been confronted by his accusers and the witnesses against him, been convicted of crime and been sentenced to punishment therefor" → he is not constitutionally entitled to another judicial determination of whether he breached the condition by committing a subsequent offense.

paras.html: Sales, quoting Fuller v. State of Alabama (45 LRA 502): the statute "supervenes to avoid the necessity for any action by the courts." The convict accepts clemency on its conditions, including that the governor may withdraw it in a certain contingency and shall himself determine when that contingency has arisen. "It is as if the convict ... had expressly contracted and agreed" that the executive order for his arrest and remandment would issue and "be conclusive upon him."

paras.html: Re: Espuelas – due process is not necessarily judicial:
paras.text: Re: Espuelas – due process is not necessarily judicial:

paras.html: "Due process is not necessarily judicial." The convict had his day in court during his trial for the original crime. The conditional pardon was a generous exercise of the Chief Executive's constitutional prerogative; acceptance carried with it the Executive's authority to determine whether a condition has been violated. "To no other department of the Government [has] such power been intrusted."

paras.html: United States v. Wilson: a conditional pardon is "in force and substance a contract" between the Executive and the grantee. Once accepted, the condition binds the State as well → it limits not only the pardonee's conduct but also the President's power of recommitment, which may be exercised only if the condition is violated.

paras.html: Revocation of amnesty requires congressional concurrence: Art. VII, Sec. 19 is silent on revocation, but “the revocation of a grant of amnesty must be with the concurrence of the Legislature”; allowing the President to revoke alone “renders futile the participation of the Legislature in its grant.” [This is stated in the body; the fallo only declares Proc. No. 572 void.]
paras.text: Revocation of amnesty requires congressional concurrence: Art. VII, Sec. 19 is silent on revocation, but “the revocation of a grant of amnesty must be with the concurrence of the Legislature”; allowing the President to revoke alone “renders futile the participation of the Legislature in its grant.” [This is stated in the body; the fallo only declares Proc. No. 572 void.]

paras.html: Amnesty may be revoked, but only within limits: Where a grant is subject to conditions that are not met, it may be revoked, but the revocation must comply with the Constitution and any procedure in the grant or its rules. The President's power of control cannot be used to revoke a DND amnesty decision that has become final and immutable.
paras.text: Amnesty may be revoked, but only within limits: Where a grant is subject to conditions that are not met, it may be revoked, but the revocation must comply with the Constitution and any procedure in the grant or its rules. The President's power of control cannot be used to revoke a DND amnesty decision that has become final and immutable.

paras.html: Effect of amnesty on a later prosecution: Where the accused moves to dismiss on the ground of amnesty, double jeopardy applies, even though the dismissal was on his motion. An executive issuance that strips a person of an amnesty violates the ex post facto clause even if it is not a penal law.

paras.html: Admission of guilt: It suffices that the applicant admits (a) committing the acts covered by the amnesty and (b) that these acts are criminal; an admission of the specific crime charged is not required.

paras.html: November 24, 2010: President Aquino issued Proclamation No. 75, granting amnesty to active and former AFP and PNP personnel and their supporters for crimes connected with the Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off, and the Manila Peninsula Incident. Sec. 1 provides:
paras.text: November 24, 2010: President Aquino issued Proclamation No. 75, granting amnesty to active and former AFP and PNP personnel and their supporters for crimes connected with the Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off, and the Manila Peninsula Incident. Sec. 1 provides:

paras.html: SECTION 1. Grant of Amnesty. — Amnesty is hereby granted to all active and former personnel of the AFP and PNP as well as their supporters who have or may have committed crimes punishable under the Revised Penal Code, the Articles of War or other laws in connection with, in relation or incident to the July 27, 2003 Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off and the November 29, 2007 Manila Peninsula Incident who shall apply therefor; Provided that amnesty shall not cover rape, acts of torture, crimes against chastity and other crimes committed for personal ends.

paras.html: G.R. No. 241494 (Trillanes v. Medialdea): On September 5, 2018, Trillanes filed with the SC a Petition for Certiorari, Prohibition, and Injunction assailing Proc. No. 572, with a prayer for a TRO/WPI. In its Injunction Resolution (September 11, 2018), the Court denied injunctive relief: whether Trillanes filed an application and admitted guilt are factual questions, so the Makati RTCs “should be given leeway in exercising their concurrent jurisdiction” over the legality of Proc. No. 572. It also took judicial notice of President Duterte's statement that Trillanes would not be arrested without a court warrant, so there was no extreme urgency.

paras.html: G.R. No. 256660 (Coup d'etat Case): Branch 148 held a full evidentiary hearing. In its Order of October 22, 2018, it found that Trillanes filed his application in the prescribed form, admitted guilt, and recanted contrary statements. It held Proc. No. 572 valid but Trillanes entitled to amnesty, and denied the Omnibus Motion (MRs of both sides denied, November 22, 2018). The People (OSG) filed an R65 petition with the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 159217). On May 31, 2021, the CA dismissed it: Proc. No. 572 is valid, but the prosecution failed to prove non-filing and non-admission. The People filed an R45 petition with the SC (June 15, 2021).

paras.html: G.R. No. 256078 (Rebellion Case): Branch 150 held only a summary hearing on affidavits and documents. In its Order of November 25, 2018 [the CA's fallo refers to the “Orders of 25 September and 18 December 2018”], it held that Proc. No. 572 did not violate Trillanes' rights, credited the Andrade Certification, found that he filed no application, declared its 2011 Dismissal Order void ab initio (so it never became final), and granted the warrant and HDO (bail at ₱200,000). MR denied (December 18, 2018). Trillanes filed an R65 petition with the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 159811); its TRO was denied. On March 1, 2021, the CA granted the petition: Proc. No. 572 is valid, but a void order must be attacked through an independent action or collaterally, not by a mere motion in the same case, and the denial of an evidentiary hearing violated due process. The Orders were set aside. The People filed an R45 petition with the SC (March 24, 2021).

paras.html: Art. VII, Sec. 19 requires concurrence for the grant but is silent on whether an amnesty may be revoked and whether the President can do so alone.
paras.text: Art. VII, Sec. 19 requires concurrence for the grant but is silent on whether an amnesty may be revoked and whether the President can do so alone.

paras.html: History: the 1935 Constitution (Art. VII, Sec. 11(6): concurrence of the National Assembly) and the 1973 Constitution (Art. VII, Sec. 11: concurrence of the Batasang Pambansa) → the two elements (presidential grant + legislative concurrence) have always remained.

paras.html: Nature: amnesty is the “general pardon to rebels for their treason and other high political offenses” (Villa v. Allen), granted to classes of persons, before or after prosecution and sometimes after conviction (Barrioquinto v. Fernandez). It has historically been granted to groups who committed crimes with political color.

Allen), granted to classes of persons, before or after prosecution and sometimes after conviction (Barrioquinto v. Fernandez). It has historically been granted to groups who committed crimes with political color.

paras.html: Effects: amnesty “looks backward and abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself”; the grantee stands as though he committed no offense; it has the force of law → farther-reaching than the general pardoning power.
paras.text: Effects: amnesty “looks backward and abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself”; the grantee stands as though he committed no offense; it has the force of law → farther-reaching than the general pardoning power.

paras.html: Purpose: it is a political tool in peace negotiations with rebel or secessionist groups and in bringing those who took up arms back into the fold.
paras.text: Purpose: it is a political tool in peace negotiations with rebel or secessionist groups and in bringing those who took up arms back into the fold.

paras.html: → Because it exempts groups from the criminal laws for a political end, its grant involves policy choices requiring the confluence of both the Executive and the Legislature. The concurrence also works as a check and balance, ensuring amnesty is not granted for one person's motives or co-opted for personal political pursuits.

paras.html: “[T]here is no doubt that an amnesty can be revoked for legitimate grounds”: where the grant is subject to conditions that are not met, it may be revoked, but the revocation must comply with the Constitution and any procedure in the grant or its rules.
paras.text: “[T]here is no doubt that an amnesty can be revoked for legitimate grounds”: where the grant is subject to conditions that are not met, it may be revoked, but the revocation must comply with the Constitution and any procedure in the grant or its rules.

paras.html: Rule: the revocation of a grant of amnesty must be with the concurrence of the Legislature. Though not stated in Sec. 19, the Court is guided by (a) giving life to the checks-and-balance function and (b) the principle that a constitutional provision must not be interpreted to render its purpose nugatory.

paras.html: Unilateral revocation “renders futile the participation of the Legislature in its grant”: the President could change his mind for personal reasons, or a successor could revoke a predecessor's grant, disregarding the Legislature's own policy choice and without letting it participate.

paras.html: A system where the President has free rein to revoke makes the grant “precarious and unreliable” and removes an important check → amnesty becomes an ineffective political tool.

paras.html: This case is a “prime example”: legislative concurrence checks both the procedure and the motives of a revocation, so revocation cannot be held “as a sword of Damocles against amnesty grantees.”

paras.html: An ex post facto law includes one that “deprives persons accused of crime of some lawful protection to which they have become entitled, such as ... the proclamation of amnesty” and every law that alters the situation of a person to his disadvantage.

paras.html: The prohibition generally targets retrospective penal laws, but in Republic v. Eugenio the Court applied it to Sec. 11 of the AMLA (bank inquiry; not penal) because it removed a layer of protection that account holders had before the law.

paras.html: The Bill of Rights protects the individual against the State → the prohibition binds all branches, including the Executive. Citing J. Caguioa's observation in the deliberations: if a law cannot deprive an accused of such a protection, neither can a presidential proclamation.

paras.html: Art. III, Sec. 21; “res judicata in prison grey.” Elements: (1) valid information; (2) competent court; (3) arraignment and plea; (4) conviction, acquittal, or dismissal without the express consent of the accused.

paras.html: Amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime: "when an accused maintains that he has not committed a crime, he cannot have any use for amnesty." It is "rank inconsistency" to seek forgiveness for an act one claims not to have committed. The contrary rule in Barrioquinto, De Los Santos, and Viray (admission not a condition precedent) has been superseded and deemed overruled by People v. Llanita and People v. Guillermo.

paras.html: Petitioners argued in their MR that they had impliedly admitted their participation in the killing. The CA held that "mere implied admission is not sufficient", because DOJ Administrative Order No. 144 (October 11, 1950), amending AO No. 179 (November 17, 1949), directs that, for offenses under the RPC (other than crimes against chastity) committed between December 8, 1941 and the liberation of the province or city, "in order that the Amnesty Commission may take cognizance of the case, the accused or respondent must allege or claim verbally or in writing that he committed the acts charged against him in furtherance of the resistance movement or against persons who aided in the war efforts of the enemy," for amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime.
